title: AI's front-runners are just oil refineries, not the native-app winners
dek: AI has entered its agent phase: the first-stage leaders are only refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organisations must move from jobs to tasks; and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to make something out of nothing.
why: Zeng Ming uses a three-stage industrial history to give you a coordinate system for where AI stands — an antidote to "this time is different" optimism, plus the window of opportunity for application founders and a brutal forecast for incumbents' transitions.
who: CEOs working on AI strategy, executives at traditional giants hunting for a second curve, AI investors, and technical founders torn between building models and building applications.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialisation of a general-purpose technology into three stages: first it becomes social infrastructure, then applications explode, and finally native applications appear. In 2026, token as a unit of measurement reaching consensus shows the first stage has matured; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called "lobster") mark AI's formal entry into the agent stage. He draws the analogy to the 1992 website-building movement: people then built websites to share information, people today build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet, and whoever can set the agent standard and seize the user entry point may hold the biggest opportunity of the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will appear, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming says plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technological and commercial achievements, but business history shows the first wave of breakout companies are most likely not the winners of the native-application stage. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, AOL was valued at $220 billion, and neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that refine the base oil — the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies, and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly exist, but not necessarily one of today's two front-runners. Model companies will move toward an oligopoly plus heavy government regulation as a mature business.

points.h: The unit of an AI-native organisation is the task, not the job
points.body: The company corresponds to the industrial age's bureaucracy; AI overturns the industrial age, and the corporate system will die out. The basic unit of an AI-native organisation is not the job but the task: people are not organised by reporting lines but flow around "what needs to be solved", and humans and AI coordinate around tasks. So well-designed jobs and hierarchies will disappear, and the traditional middle layer will die out too; future founders must first define the organisation's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organisational form, and OpenAI itself is more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of the new organisation is more like a sports team, emphasising transparency, sharing and co-creation, no longer relying on commands and appraisals.

points.h: Excellence is only judged afterwards; being good is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming argues that "good ≠ great". Being good is growth that keeps getting positive feedback, while greatness requires overcoming negative feedback again and again, persisting when no one approves, and finally proving through enormous success that you were the era's prophet — which is why "greatness is judged after the fact". Good people fall easily into a loop of proving themselves, which makes their strategies conservative. Great people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the times and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders he asks, "Ten years from now, what kind of self would you be satisfied with?" If the answer is "a ten-billion-dollar company", that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly great founders tend to be altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era can't be planned, only generated
points.body: Strategy in the AI era is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": the organisation must build an environment and network in which strategic insight emerges naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are higher, a CEO cannot plan by linear extrapolation, nor outsource strategy to McKinsey — McKinsey's explosion was a product of the industrial age's slow maturation. His methodology is "look ten years out, think three years out, act one year out", with the core being "think three years out": you must at least see two or three milestones, creating tension between short-term action and the mid-term picture. Organisation-building must guarantee enough context rather than control, letting the right people make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robotics is still in a phase of strategic exploration, far from convergence. The two current paths — build a generalised brain first, or close the loop on scenarios first — are both logically valid, and no one can judge in advance which is faster. By historical analogy, the car industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and only entered scale when Ford built the assembly line in 1913; robots have not yet had their Model T moment, and whoever actually sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But the better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented came countless categories — refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners — and robots interacting with the physical world will have N kinds of big scenarios, with home, companionship and industry each potentially producing their own native giant.

points.h: The incumbents who feel safe are the least safe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a huge wave no one is safe, and feeling safe is the most unsafe thing of all. In business history no era's companies have ever transitioned smoothly into the next era; IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that overturns the industrial revolution, not a continuity innovation like mobile internet, so old giants' technical reserves and organisational culture are negative assets. Google can live on as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is likewise not naturally safe. The new platform will most likely be created by a new company.

points.h: Human value lies in making something from nothing, not in writing songs or painting
points.body: Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI, and people are on one hand forced and on the other finally liberated to develop new potential. That potential is called creativity — not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and make something out of nothing. AI has already taken away all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. That is why he calls his own mission "to be a happy researcher", and believes civilisation's next step will reorganise around creativity, with even the education system forced to shift from "instilling knowledge" to "open exploration", because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

quotes.text: The most successful companies are always contrarian, but being contrarian doesn't guarantee success.
It may not survive to the end. It will probably do quite well going forward, but it is most likely not a big player, a big winner, in the native-application stage.
First-stage companies struggle to survive into the second stage, and second-stage companies struggle to survive into the third.
So companies will disappear, companies will die out. There's nothing to regret about that. There'll be more fun things ahead — how many people are happy going to work at a company now? Not happy.

My technology is so good, I created so much value, why might my company be worth nothing? Because of the basic laws of economics: as long as supply is homogeneous, you cannot capture high profits, and you are a company that isn't worth much.

Greatness is judged after the fact, because you overcame negative feedback again and again, and when everyone disapproved of you, you finally proved through enormous success that you were the era's earliest prophet.
I have always believed that in the face of a huge wave no one is safe, and whoever feels safe is the least safe.
